t: The Nahda, the “awakening”, was a movement of 19th-century Arab writers, translators and teachers, Muslim and Christian, who sought to renew Arabic culture and join it to modern knowledge.
Through printing presses, newspapers, journals, dictionaries, schools and translations, centred in Cairo and Beirut, they created modern Arabic prose and Arabic journalism, drama and the novel.
Its thinkers debated the reform of religion, government and education and the place of women, and their ideas fed both Islamic modernism and Arab nationalism.
dyk: The first play in Arabic, Marun al-Naqqash’s al-Bakhil (The Miser), adapted from Molière, was performed in Beirut in 1847; by 1850 he had built a theatre near his home for a new play drawn from the Thousand and One Nights.
ev: Muhammad Ali founds a government press at Bulaq, near Cairo, which prints its first book in 1822
Rifa’a al-Tahtawi goes to Paris as imam of an Egyptian student mission; his account of France appears in 1834
Marun al-Naqqash stages al-Bakhil in Beirut, the first play in Arabic
Butrus al-Bustani founds the National School in Beirut, open to pupils of every religion
The newspaper al-Ahram begins publication in Alexandria and the journal al-Muqtataf in Beirut
Jurji Zaydan founds al-Hilal in Cairo; Hind Nawfal launches al-Fatat, the first Arabic magazine for women
Muhammad Abduh becomes Grand Mufti of Egypt; Qasim Amin publishes The Liberation of Women
The Ottoman constitution is restored, loosening censorship, and the Egyptian University opens in Cairo

f.where: Egypt and the Ottoman Levant, above all Cairo, Alexandria, Beirut, Damascus and Aleppo, with echoes in Tunis, Baghdad and Istanbul and among Arab emigrants in Paris and the Americas
f.period: c. 1820–1914: from the government press at Bulaq and the first student missions to Europe to the First World War; some historians begin it with the French invasion of Egypt in 1798, others carry it into the 1930s
f.figures: Rifa’a al-Tahtawi, Butrus al-Bustani, Ahmad Faris al-Shidyaq, Muhammad Abduh, Qasim Amin, Jurji Zaydan
f.outcome: A modern Arabic prose, press and publishing, new schools and literary forms, the reform of Islamic thought and the first expressions of Arab national feeling
